questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of campaign finance disclosure and its limits.
questions.stem: A client asks what campaign finance disclosure is actually for, in a district where a single donation funded most of one candidate's publicity. Explain the purpose of disclosure and what it can and cannot achieve.

answer.exemplar: Disclosure exists so that the sources of money in an election can be traced and judged. Reporting who gave, how much and what the money was spent on converts an invisible process into something the public, the regulator and rival parties can examine. In a small district where one donor paid for most of the publicity, disclosure would at least reveal that dependence, and the question it then raises is whether one donor's interest should shape the outcome. What disclosure cannot do is set a limit on the spending or on the influence of the donor. It is an information measure, and its value depends on what follows from the information: a limit, a reporting requirement, or a debate in the council about whether a candidate who is beholden to one funder can credibly represent the whole district.

questions.explanation: Disclosure makes the sources of election money visible so that they can be examined and debated. It is an information measure, and by itself it neither limits spending nor prevents the influence it reveals.
questions.hint: Ask what changes when the money becomes visible.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess a claim that action committees substitute for disclosure rules.
questions.stem: A campaign finance reviewer argues that action committees, which can raise and spend money in support of a ballot measure without disclosing donors, are a more flexible tool than formal disclosure rules. Evaluate the argument for a policy brief.

answer.exemplar: The argument trades one kind of transparency for another and the trade is not as favourable as it appears. A committee structure can be genuinely useful: it lets a group of people work together on a single question, and it can be funded at low cost without the apparatus of a full campaign. But the reason the reviewer likes it is precisely the feature that should worry a policy brief. A committee that spends money to influence an election or a ballot measure while naming no donors removes the one thing disclosure rules are designed to produce, which is the ability to connect a campaign's message to whoever is paying for it. Where money is substantial, that is where the risk of a narrow interest being concealed lies. The honest comparison is between two routes to the same political outcome, one of which records its financial support and one of which does not, and the flexibility argument does not make the second route safer. If committees are to be permitted, the better answer is to require disclosure from them rather than to treat them as an exemption.

questions.explanation: The argument values the feature that matters most, that donors are not named, and calls it flexibility. If committees are allowed, the better answer is to require disclosure from them rather than to exempt them.
questions.hint: Ask what the disclosure rules are for.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how registration arrangements shape the composition of those who vote.
questions.stem: In the neighbourhood covered by your brief, residents must register separately for a local election, and a small team of volunteers has been helping with the forms. Explain how registration arrangements affect the composition of those who vote.

answer.exemplar: Registration is a filter placed before the ballot, and every requirement attached to it selects for some people and against others. A separate application with documentary proof removes anyone who lacks the documents, cannot find a registrar within opening hours, or has recently moved without knowing that the record must be updated. A recently arrived resident is the clearest case, because the administrative habit of registering is a habit acquired over years. The composition of those who vote then reflects who can complete a process, not who has the strongest interest in the issues on the ballot. A volunteer helping with forms is a partial remedy, and it can widen participation, but it also introduces a further condition, namely that the volunteer is available and willing. Automatic registration through existing records removes the step entirely, and the council's design brief should treat any manual step as a cost borne by the people least well able to pay it.

questions.explanation: Every registration requirement filters who can reach the ballot, so the electorate reflects who can complete a process. Volunteer help widens access, but the deeper fix is to remove the registration step altogether.
questions.hint: Ask who the paperwork excludes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the mechanisms through which incumbency advantage operates.
questions.stem: Explain, for a design brief on district representation, the different ways in which holding an office already gives its holder an advantage in the next election.

answer.exemplar: The advantage operates through several channels at once, and they are worth separating because some can be reduced by design and others cannot. The most obvious is the record: an incumbent can point to completed work, and a challenger can only promise. The second is name recognition, which is cheaper for the holder to maintain than for the challenger to acquire, since a challenger must build a profile from nothing while the incumbent is already known. The third is organisation, in the form of a functioning committee, a contact list and a record of who supports what, all of which take years to build. The fourth is the ability to shape the agenda, deciding which questions are put to the council and which are left out, which alters what voters are choosing between. The fifth is the deterrence of opponents, since a challenger must weigh the risk of running against a sitting member with an established reputation. Design measures that make challengers' route easier, such as candidate support for first-time candidates or a limit on the resources an incumbent can draw on the office, address the organisational channels but not the record or the agenda.

questions.explanation: Incumbency works through the record, name recognition, organisation, agenda control and the deterrence of challengers. Some can be reduced by design, but the record and the agenda cannot be removed from the office.
questions.hint: Ask what the holder already has and the challenger does not.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Design a boundary process that resists partisan manipulation of district lines.
questions.stem: Your brief asks for a boundary review process that produces districts which do not distort representation, regardless of which party controls the commission. Propose a process and justify how it resists manipulation.

answer.exemplar: The difficulty with boundary review is that the person drawing the lines can choose whether they help or harm their own party, and every technical rule leaves room for that choice. The most effective guard is to take the discretion out of the hands of the drafter. First, fix the data and the formula before the drafter is appointed, so the commission cannot select which inputs to use. Second, use a small set of neutral criteria stated in advance, such as equal population within a stated tolerance, contiguity, and a requirement to avoid splitting established communities, and require the commission to publish a map for each rejected alternative so that the choices can be inspected. Third, make the commission independent of party officers and of any department with an interest in the outcome, and give it a public timetable with hearings in every affected ward. Fourth, build in a review after the first election under the new boundaries, so that the design can be corrected from evidence rather than from argument.

questions.explanation: Distortion survives wherever the drafter keeps discretion, so data and criteria must be fixed in advance. Publishing rejected alternatives and a review after one election allow correction from evidence, not argument.
questions.hint: Take discretion away from the drafter.

questions.learningObjective: Explain what lobbyist registration achieves and where it falls short.
questions.stem: A client asks how far a public register of lobbyists would strengthen the council's decision-making, and what problems it would leave unsolved. Explain.

answer.exemplar: A register of lobbyists is a transparency measure with a narrow but genuine target. Requiring the name of every person who approaches a member on behalf of a client, together with the client and the subject of the meeting, turns a private arrangement into a matter of record. That matters in two specific ways. A member can no longer treat an approach as a personal favour, and a resident can see whether a decision was shaped by a paid interest rather than a public argument. The limits are equally clear. A register records who spoke, not what they said or what was promised in return, so the influence itself stays hidden. A registration requirement also says nothing about unequal access, since a well-resourced firm can register several lobbyists and attend more meetings than a small organisation can, which makes the register a record of presence rather than of pressure. The register is therefore a necessary floor rather than a solution, and it works best when combined with a record of the material left with members.

questions.explanation: Registration records who spoke for whom, which makes a private approach a matter of record. It does not show what was said or promised, and it does not equalise access.
questions.hint: Ask what the register cannot show.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Parties as the route to office
questions.learningObjective: Explain the consequences of parties being the only route to public office.
questions.stem: Explain, for a policy brief, what follows for electoral competition when political parties are the only route by which a citizen can reach public office.

answer.exemplar: If parties are the only route, three things follow. The first is that parties become gatekeepers of political ambition, and the question of who can stand for office becomes a decision taken inside the organisation rather than one taken by the electorate. The second is that parties acquire a reason to prioritise those who will work within the machine, because a candidate who is a loyal and effective member is worth more to the party than an independent figure who might take a different line. The third is that voters' choices are constrained to the parties' candidates, so the range of programmes on offer is decided before the election rather than during it. None of this is a call to abolish parties, which perform functions no other body performs. But the design brief should ask what mechanisms would offset the gatekeeping, such as nomination rules that allow members to be placed on a list without senior approval, a cap on how many seats a party may contest uncontested, and a requirement that parties publish their nomination criteria so that the treatment of candidates can be examined.

questions.explanation: Making parties the only route makes them gatekeepers of who may stand, and rewards loyal insiders. It also fixes the range of programmes before the vote, so nomination rules and published criteria matter.
questions.hint: Ask who decides who may stand.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of action committees and the difficulty they create for disclosure.
questions.stem: Set out, for a policy brief, what an action committee is, why such bodies exist, and how their status creates a difficulty for disclosure rules.

answer.exemplar: An action committee is a group formed around a single question, most often a ballot measure, which raises money and campaigns for one outcome. The reason such bodies exist is that the alternatives are cumbersome. A registered party must organise a candidate, build a list, and accept obligations that extend well beyond the question at issue. A committee can be formed in a fortnight, it can be dissolved once the question is decided, and it can be funded by people who agree with the outcome without wanting to join an organisation. That flexibility is a genuine public benefit, and it is the reason informal bodies existed long before any disclosure regime was drafted. The difficulty is that the same flexibility means the money can arrive without a paper trail. If a committee is formed to run an intense campaign on one measure, the questions it answers are consequential, and the people who finance it may have interests that would be visible if they were named. The resolution most regimes reach is to require disclosure from committees above a stated threshold of spending, on the reasoning that ordinary amounts do not warrant the administrative burden while substantial amounts do.

questions.explanation: Committees exist because they campaign on one question with a speed a party cannot offer. That flexibility can carry substantial money without a paper trail, which is why disclosure thresholds are used.
questions.hint: Ask why a party cannot do the same work.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Design measures that reduce unequal participation across a borough.
questions.stem: Your brief sets out a plan to raise participation in the borough's low-turnout wards without making the scheme harder for those already engaged. Propose measures and justify the trade-offs they involve.

answer.exemplar: Start from the diagnosis rather than from a campaign, because the measures that work depend on which barrier is binding. Where the barrier is administrative, the answer is to remove the step: automatic registration from existing council records, the ability to register at any point including on polling day, and a roll that follows households rather than requiring them to follow the register. Where the barrier is physical, the answer is to bring the poll closer: additional polling places in large estates, mobile booths at community venues on the day, and postal voting for those who cannot travel. Where the barrier is informational, the answer is cheap and should not be forgotten: a clear timetable, a reminder card that names the local polling station, and targeted contact through schools and housing associations. Two general points apply. Measures that target a ward by name risk stigmatising its residents, so a programme should be described in terms of the barrier it removes. And any measure that simplifies registration must be paired with a contact route for those with no fixed address, or it will improve the statistics at the expense of the people hardest to reach.

questions.explanation: The right measure depends on which barrier binds, and administrative, physical and informational obstacles differ. Framing around barriers avoids stigma, and easier registration needs a route for the hardest to reach.
questions.hint: Diagnose the barrier before choosing the measure.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the main sources of unequal turnout across a constituency.
questions.stem: Using the figures in your brief, explain the main sources of unequal turnout across the borough, and explain why a single participation rate is a poor measure of the borough's political health.

answer.exemplar: Three sources account for most of the gap. The first is administrative: where the register must be applied for and updated, people who have moved, arrived recently or simply never registered remain on the roll but not on the list, and they never reach the poll. The second is physical: the cost of getting to a polling place, which is small in a compact district and substantial in a large rural ward without transport, falls hardest on those with least money and no vehicle. The third is informational, and it is the cheapest to fix: many voters do not know that a local election is held on a different day from the national one, or where their polling station is, and the borough's turnout fell in the years when that information was not communicated. A single participation rate conceals all three, because it averages a well-served area and a poorly served one into a figure that describes neither. It also makes change difficult to see, since a modest gain in a well-served ward can offset a substantial loss in a poorly served one. Reporting turnout by ward, and alongside it the gap between the best and worst served areas, gives a truer account of the borough's political health.

questions.explanation: Administrative barriers, the cost of reaching the poll, and lack of information together produce the gap. A single rate conceals all three, so ward-level reporting is needed to see real change.
questions.hint: Ask what the average smooths over.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Design a disclosure regime that reveals influence without stranding candidates.
questions.stem: Your brief asks for a campaign finance disclosure scheme suitable for a small borough where most campaigns are inexpensive. Propose a scheme and justify how it balances transparency against administrative burden.

answer.exemplar: Scale the scheme to the money, and the small borough's problem largely dissolves. Many disclosure regimes are designed for national campaigns, and they fail in small contests because the reporting burden is the same whatever is spent. A tiered scheme solves this. At the lowest tier, where spending is negligible, a candidate files a simple one-page return with the total raised and spent, with no donor list, and the cost of compliance is a few minutes. At a middle tier, donor names are required for donations above a modest sum, and a running register is kept. At the top tier, the full regime applies: all donors above a small floor, a spending breakdown by category, and a statement of any non-financial support. Two design details matter as much as the tiers. The return should be published in a single indexed register that is searchable by candidate and date, so that a member of the public can check a claim without knowing which committee or party to ask. And the rule should require disclosure of in-kind support, because in a small contest a free hall, a printing run and a mailing list can be worth more than a donation, and those are the supports most likely to go unrecorded.

questions.explanation: A tiered scheme matches burden to money, so small campaigns are not strangled by national-scale rules. One searchable register and disclosure of in-kind support close the two gaps that make returns incomplete.
questions.hint: Match the burden to the size of the campaign.

questions.learningObjective: Assess a proposal to reduce the advantages enjoyed by sitting members.
questions.stem: A proposal in your district would bar sitting members from using council resources in their campaigns and would require them to publish a full list of their campaign spending. Evaluate the proposal for the design brief.

answer.exemplar: The two measures are well aimed, and they are not equally effective, so the proposal deserves support with a qualification. The restriction on council resources attacks the clearest misuse, because a member who spends public money on posters, mailings and staff is spending the resources of the district to compete for its office, and no reasonable defence survives contact with that fact. It also removes a channel through which the office manufactures the very familiarity that the advantage rests on. The disclosure requirement is more modest, because a sitting member's spending is already visible to anyone who watches the council, so the new rule may record what is obvious rather than reveal what is hidden. What neither measure touches is the harder advantage: the record of completed work, the contacts accumulated in office, and the control of the council's agenda. Those are produced by holding the office rather than by spending money on it, and a candidate cannot be given the office and then charged with the experience it confers. A useful addition to the proposal would be a limit on the length of consecutive terms, which addresses the accumulated advantages at their source.

questions.explanation: Banning council resources attacks a real misuse, while an incumbent spending register records what is visible. Neither touches the advantages produced by holding office, which a limit on consecutive terms would address.
questions.hint: Ask which advantage each measure actually reaches.

questions.learningObjective: State what a threshold rule produces for the coverage of disclosure.
questions.stem: A rule requires action committees that spend above a threshold to register and disclose donors, and exempts smaller groups entirely. Which arrangement does this produce?

options.text: Full transparency, because any group that matters will exceed the threshold.
options.misconception: assumes every significant group exceeds a stated threshold

options.text: Partial transparency, since disclosure reaches the larger campaigns and not the numerous small ones.
No transparency, because the largest campaigns always find ways around registration.
options.misconception: asserts evasion without any evidence in the scenario

options.text: Uniform transparency, because the threshold applies the same test to every committee.
options.misconception: treats a common test as equivalent coverage

questions.explanation: A threshold produces partial coverage by design: campaigns above it are recorded and campaigns below it are not, and small campaigns are typically the more numerous. The rule therefore creates a visible record of the largest spending without a complete picture.
questions.hint: Ask which campaigns the rule actually reaches.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Read the operation of a register of interests from an extract.

stimulus.body: Extract from the council's register of interests: 'The register records 61 entries, of which 44 relate to persons registered to lobby on behalf of clients. The remaining 17 entries are declarations of councillor interests made under the standing orders. Each lobbyist entry names the registered individual and the client organisation, and the notes column records the general subject of recent approaches. The register's introduction states that the notes are compiled by the members themselves and are not a record of any statement made to them, and that entries are retained for two years.'

questions.stem: What does the extract show about the operation of the register?

options.text: That the register records everything said to members, since it notes recent approaches in detail.
options.misconception: reads a subject note as a record of statements

options.text: That the register is the principal source of information about councillors' own interests.
options.misconception: mistakes the councillor entries for the larger group

options.text: That it identifies lobbyists and their clients, while recording only a general subject of approaches.
That every entry is permanent, since the council keeps them for the electoral record.
options.misconception: contradicts the stated two-year retention

questions.explanation: The register names each lobbyist and client and gives only a general subject for recent approaches, and the introduction states plainly that it is not a record of statements made. It therefore identifies who spoke for whom only.
questions.hint: Read what the introduction says the notes are not.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Draw a strategic conclusion from a survey of reasons for not voting.

stimulus.body: Survey finding for the consultation: 'Asked why they had not voted at the last local election, respondents gave the following reasons in order of frequency: 41 per cent said they were not aware there was an election, 22 per cent said the polling place was too far to reach, 14 per cent said they had moved and did not know they had to re-register, 11 per cent said they were working and could not get time off, and the remaining respondents gave other reasons. In the previous cycle the leading reason had been lack of awareness, at 46 per cent.'

questions.stem: What does the survey finding suggest about the direction of a turnout strategy?

options.text: That information campaigns have already achieved all they can, since awareness is improving.
options.misconception: reads a small improvement as a completed campaign

options.text: That the dominant obstacle is now physical, since awareness has fallen sharply.
options.misconception: assumes awareness fell when the figure moved the other way

options.text: That re-registration drives almost all non-voting, and should be the sole focus.
options.misconception: inflates one reason into the dominant one

options.text: That awareness remains the largest obstacle but has shrunk, so it still matters and other barriers now weigh more.

questions.explanation: Lack of awareness is still the most common reason at 41 per cent, though it has fallen from 46. The rest now comes from distance, registration and work, so the strategy should widen as well as continue.
questions.hint: Compare this year's reasons with last year's.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the effect of a rolling update requirement on the roll.
questions.stem: Your brief notes that electoral registration is a rolling process, so a voter who moves within the borough must update the record before they can vote at the new address. What is the effect of that requirement?

options.text: It creates a recurring chance for eligible voters to be removed from the roll by oversight.
It guarantees that the roll contains every eligible resident of the borough.
options.misconception: assumes a rolling process eliminates all gaps

options.text: It means a voter may register at any polling place on the day of the election.
options.misconception: confuses a rolling update process with same-day registration

options.text: It gives the electoral service a duty to visit households that have moved.
options.misconception: invents a door-to-door duty the rule does not mention

questions.explanation: A recurring update requirement means every move inside the borough creates a fresh opportunity for the record to fall out of date. An outdated record excludes a voter until corrected, generating continuous non-participation.
questions.hint: Ask what a move does to the record.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Parties as the route to office
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the case for requiring party affiliation for public office.
questions.stem: A proposal in your district would allow candidates to stand without any party affiliation. Evaluate the case for and against the change for a policy brief.

answer.exemplar: The case for the change is that a party requirement narrows the field in a way that has nothing to do with governing. A candidate who has spent years organising neighbourhood action, or who commands the confidence of a small and engaged electorate, may be kept off the ballot because a party's local committee will not approve a nomination, and the reason is usually not a matter of merit. The case against is equally substantial. Parties are the only bodies that commit to a programme, maintain a list of candidates across a whole district, and absorb the cost of a campaign, and if unaffiliated candidates can reach the ballot without providing any of that, the effect may be a crowded ballot of people who cannot sustain a campaign to its conclusion. There is also a party-side argument that an unaffiliated candidate who wins cannot be replaced by a successor from the same label, because there is no label. The change is therefore not obviously an opening, and a middle course may serve better: permit unaffiliated candidacy with a modest deposit that is returned if the candidate wins a modest share of the vote, and require party nominations to be approved by a published procedure so that the gatekeeping is at least visible.

questions.explanation: The case for rests on merit and openness, the case against on parties' capacity to sustain programmes. A modest deposit and published nomination procedures capture much of the benefit without losing that capacity.
questions.hint: Ask what parties provide that individuals cannot.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State what a disclosure scheme requires above its floor.

stimulus.body: From the regulator's guidance: 'Where a donor is a company, the return must name the company and state the nature of its business. Where a donor is a trust, the return must name the trustees and the beneficial owners of the trust property. Where a donor is a body formed to advance a political aim, the return must name the individual who controls it. A donor may be described as anonymous only where the sum given is below the disclosure floor, and any anonymous donation above that floor must be declared as an amount without a name.'

questions.stem: According to the guidance, what does the scheme require?

options.text: That all donations, however small, must be declared by name.
options.misconception: ignores the floor below which anonymity is permitted

options.text: That donations above the floor must be attributable to a named person or organisation.
That only donations from companies and trusts are subject to the disclosure rules.
options.misconception: ignores the rule on politically formed bodies

options.text: That donors may remain anonymous provided they are not businesses or trusts.
options.misconception: treats anonymity as a matter of the donor's type

questions.explanation: Above the floor the guidance pushes disclosure all the way to the person who controls a donor, so a payment cannot be made anonymously by routing it through a vehicle. Below the floor anonymity is allowed, which is why the floor matters.
questions.hint: Read who must ultimately be named.

questions.learningObjective: Identify what a population criterion fails to measure about a boundary.
questions.stem: A boundary commission's draft splits a large city ward into three districts, and the resulting map is described by one commissioner as making sense because every district now has a similar population. What does that reasoning overlook?

options.text: The fact that the ward is large and could have been left as a single district.
options.misconception: reads a stated justification as a rebuttal to it

options.text: The rule that districts must also be contiguous with one another.
options.misconception: invents a contiguity rule the scenario does not mention

options.text: That equal population says nothing about how the city's votes are distributed among the districts.
The number of polling places needed to serve the three new districts.
options.misconception: introduces an administrative factor the commissioner never raised

questions.explanation: Equal population is a real criterion, but it says nothing about how the votes of the original ward are then spread across the districts that replace it. A map can satisfy the population rule and still be drawn to advantage one party.
questions.hint: Ask what the criterion fails to measure.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Support a conclusion about campaign experience from a research note.

stimulus.body: Research note on a repeated ward: 'The sitting councillor has held the seat for four consecutive elections, the most recent with 41 per cent of the vote against 39 for her challenger. A second ward, with a different profile, was won by a challenger standing for the third time with 44 per cent against 38 for a first-time candidate. The note observes that the incumbent in the first ward was on the ballot at a count of 640 voters in a ward of 2,900 electors, while the second ward's count involved 1,180 voters in 3,400 electors, and that the second ward's challenger had contested three elections with paid publicity in each.'

questions.stem: On the basis of the note, which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The first ward's incumbent is stronger than the second ward's challenger, since she won more votes.
options.misconception: compares vote totals across wards with different electorates

options.text: Repeated candidates lose, since the only challenger with experience still lost the seat.
options.misconception: reads one close result as a rule about experience

options.text: Turnout in the first ward was too low for the result to be legitimate.
options.misconception: treats a low turnout as evidence of an illegitimate result

options.text: Experience of repeated campaigns is an advantage, and it can offset a first-time candidate's disadvantage.

questions.explanation: The third-time challenger came close in a ward with far higher turnout, which is what repeated campaigning and paid publicity would deliver, and a first-time candidate began from behind. Experience of this kind is a real advantage.
questions.hint: Compare the two campaigns, not the two vote totals.

questions.learningObjective: Identify what a disclosure duty achieves without changing a group's status.
questions.stem: A rule requires a committee that spends above a threshold to disclose donors but does not require the committee to register as a party or to accept the obligations that follow. What has been achieved?

options.text: Transparency about funding, without the machinery or constraints of party status.
Full equality between committees and parties, since both now face disclosure rules.
options.misconception: assumes disclosure removes all other differences between the two

options.text: A guarantee that committees cannot spend more than parties may spend.
options.misconception: infers a spending ceiling from a disclosure duty

options.text: A means of holding committees to the same accounting rules as the electoral commission.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Design a lobbyist registration scheme suited to a local authority.
questions.stem: Your brief asks for a lobbyist registration scheme for a borough council that is small, informal and reliant on councillors doing much of their own research. Propose a scheme and justify how it fits the council's circumstances.

answer.exemplar: The scheme should be proportionate to a council where a handful of people make the decisions, and it should be built around the risk that matters here, which is that a decision affecting one street or one business is made in conversation rather than in committee. A short register, published online and updated within a week of any approach, is enough: the lobbyist's name, the client, the member approached and the general subject. Two further features make the scheme work. It should apply to anyone who approaches a member on behalf of someone else, including a trade association's volunteer, because the exemption for volunteers is the usual way a scheme is defeated, and it should not apply to a resident speaking for themselves, since the right of residents to petition is not a lobbying practice. The scheme should also record the outcome rather than only the approach, with a note of what the member did with the representation, which converts a register of conversations into a record of influence. Enforcement should be light, with a warning for a first failure and a requirement to remove the entry from the register for a persistent one. In a small council the risk of over-formality is real, and a scheme that people avoid because it is cumbersome will record far less than a simple one that they use.

questions.explanation: A small council needs a short, current register covering volunteers too, with outcomes recorded to trace influence. Light enforcement suits the scale and avoids a scheme that people avoid and therefore defeat.
questions.hint: Build the scheme around the local risk.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State carefully what a co-varying pair of measures establishes.
questions.stem: Your brief finds that in the borough's most deprived ward, 19 per cent of residents are citizens of another country, while in the least deprived ward the figure is 4 per cent, and turnout follows the same pattern. What is the most careful statement of the relationship?

options.text: Citizenship status causes the turnout difference, because foreign citizens are not permitted to vote.
options.misconception: assumes a franchise rule the brief does not state

options.text: The two measures vary together, which suggests a link but does not establish the direction of causation.
Turnout falls as the foreign-born share rises, which proves that newcomers vote less.
options.misconception: treats a correlation as a proved cause

options.text: The turnout gap is unrelated to citizenship, because the ward boundaries are drawn to exclude new arrivals.
options.misconception: asserts a boundary motive the brief never suggests

questions.explanation: Citizenship composition and turnout move together, a reason to investigate rather than a demonstration. The gap may reflect registration, unfamiliarity or deprivation, and the brief does not separate them.
questions.hint: Ask whether the brief establishes a cause.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the intended effect of marking the roll at the polling place.
questions.stem: An electoral commission proposes that a small number of people at each polling place check the names on the roll and mark those who have already voted. What is the intended effect?

options.misconception: mistakes a record-keeping step for a counting method

options.text: To reduce the cost of the election, since fewer officials are needed at the close.
options.misconception: assumes fewer officials follow from a record of who voted

options.text: To prevent people voting more than once, by recording who has already been marked.
To compile a list of non-voters, so that they can be written to before the next election.

questions.hint: Ask what the mark is used to detect.

questions.topic: Parties as the route to office
questions.learningObjective: Explain how party affiliation is recorded and certified.

stimulus.body: Observation at the count in your district: 'The returning officer recorded that three parties contested the ward. The seat was won by the candidate of the largest party with 44 per cent of the vote, ahead of the second party's candidate on 31 per cent. A separate candidate, standing without party affiliation, took 14 per cent. The officer noted that the unaffiliated candidate's nomination papers had been submitted eleven weeks before the close of nominations, while the parties' candidates had filed three weeks earlier, and that the returning officer had been asked to read the affiliation box on each nomination paper and record what was written there.'

questions.stem: What does the note indicate about the way party affiliation operates here?

options.text: That party candidates have a legal advantage, since the officer records the affiliation box.
options.misconception: infers a legal advantage from an administrative instruction

options.text: That the unaffiliated candidate's earlier filing gives them a procedural advantage in the count.
options.misconception: treats an earlier filing as an advantage at the count

options.text: That the unaffiliated candidate won a quarter of the vote, which is a substantial showing.
options.misconception: inflates a 14 per cent share into a substantial one

options.text: That affiliation is recorded administratively at nomination, which is how parties are certified to contest.

questions.explanation: Affiliation is captured on the nomination paper and read by the officer, certifying the party to contest. The individual gains no legal privilege from it, and a 14 per cent share is modest rather than substantial.
questions.hint: Ask where affiliation is recorded.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Design disclosure and enforcement rules for local political donations.
questions.stem: Your brief requires a scheme for disclosing and limiting political donations in a borough where most campaigns cost under two thousand pounds. Propose rules and justify how they would deter hidden influence without stranding candidates.

answer.exemplar: Two principles should govern the scheme. The first is that the rules should bite where the money is, and in a small borough that means the small sums, because a hundred donations of fifty pounds are cheap to make and can be made quietly by many people acting together. So the disclosure floor should be low, set at a level below the cost of a candidate's smallest poster, and every donation above it must be named. The second is that the rules should attach to influence rather than to party identity, because the interest of a contractor in a planning decision is the same whatever the contractor's politics. Declare any meeting between a member and an interested party in a public note, and require a member to declare a direct financial interest in an item before the vote. Enforcement should be proportionate and automatic. A return filed late should be published late with a visible flag, and a candidate who fails to file should lose the right to appear in the ballot paper's official statements, which is a sanction that falls on the candidate and not on the constituency. Finally, a small public fund for campaign costs, financed from a levy on the declared donations, keeps money in the open and gives candidates a reason to disclose, because money received through the fund is money they do not have to explain.

questions.explanation: Low thresholds and rules attached to interest rather than party catch the small sums that dominate locally. Candidate-facing sanctions and a public fund make disclosure the cheaper option for honest candidates.
questions.hint: Set the threshold where the money actually is.

questions.stem: Your brief describes a boundary that places a small town entirely inside a district dominated by a different group of voters. What electoral effect does that configuration have?

options.text: The district becomes geographically incoherent, because the town is separated from the rest.
